subject: chemistry
title: Chemical Analysis Adventure: Flames, Precipitates, Machines
welcome_lead: Today you'll identify ions with flame tests, precipitates and instruments.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry stretch — flame test colours, NaOH precipitate colours for metal ions, and the strengths of instrumental analysis.
final_note: You learned the flame test colours, the NaOH precipitate colours, and why instruments beat eyeballs.

concepts.def: Heat sample on wire — colour reveals the metal ion
Insoluble solid formed when two solutions mix
Identifies metal ions by precipitate colour
Detects very small amounts of a substance
Result is very close to the true value

walkthroughs.body_html:
Dip a clean nichrome wire in the sample and hold it in a roaring Bunsen flame.

Li⁺ crimson red · Na⁺ yellow · K⁺ lilac · Ca²⁺ orange-red · Cu²⁺ green/blue-green.

Drawback: if two ions are present, a strong colour (sodium yellow) can hide the others.

Add sodium hydroxide solution to a metal ion solution — a coloured precipitate forms.

Cu²⁺ → blue precipitate. Fe²⁺ → green precipitate. Fe³⁺ → brown precipitate.

(Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ all give white precipitates — distinguish them by other tests.)

Instrumental methods (flame emission spectroscopy, mass spectrometry) beat lab tests because they are:

Fast — results in seconds. Sensitive — detect tiny traces. Accurate — very close to the true value. Small samples — only milligrams needed. Downsides: expensive kit and trained operators.
